title: You've been putting it off
hookLine: Marcus: remember how long you've delayed, and that your time has a limit (Meditations 2.4)
tomorrow: as if it were the last

cards: Everybody has a list. The call to the old friend. The doctor's appointment.

The drawer, the will, the apology, the book you swore you'd start. It's been there so long it's practically furniture; you don't even see it anymore. And each time you pass it, a small voice says, soon.
Long ago, a Roman emperor had the same list and the same voice, and in his notebook he turned around and argued with it. Today, you've been putting it off.

teach.h: HOW LONG HAVE YOU PUT IT OFF?
teach.b: Book two, section four, begins in George Long's translation: "Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it."
Notice who he's talking to. Not his generals, not his son. Himself.
The emperor, with an army at his command, is scolding himself for procrastinating. What things? He doesn't list them, and it isn't paperwork.
The passage points inward, to the work of living by reason, calm and just, which he kept meaning to get serious about.

teach.h: A LIMIT OF TIME IS FIXED.
teach.b: Then it turns: understand what kind of universe you're part of, and remember that a limit of time is fixed for you.

If you don't use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will go, and you will go, and it will not come back. That's the Stoic move. They didn't think about death to be gloomy; they thought about it to wake up.

teach.h: NOT GLOOM: A CLOCK YOU CAN HEAR.
teach.b: The limit isn't a threat; it's a clock you can finally hear. Other traditions have their own versions. The Psalms ask God to teach us to number our days.

The Buddha's last words, in the old accounts, urge his followers to strive on with diligence. Marcus puts it bluntly: you've had chance after chance, and the chances are not endless. And here's the gentle part.
He doesn't call himself a failure for putting it off. He just says, remember.
The list is still there, today still counts, and there is a limit, and you're inside it now.

how: Readers of the Meditations often return to 2.4 as a morning reminder, and some in modern Stoic practice keep a short daily reflection on the limits of time, sometimes called memento mori.

games.q: you're emperor, and you notice you've been putting off the work of living well for years. what do you do?
o: decide to start after the war.
write yourself a reminder that your time has a limit.
games.why: Marcus writes it down: remember how long you've delayed, and that a limit of time is fixed. not a threat, a wake-up.

practice: Let your list come to mind and choose one item that's waited far too long, something small enough to begin today. Picture the first step actually happening: the text typed, the number dialed, the drawer open.
Then decide exactly when you'll do it, and say the time inside.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, scolding himself in his notebook for putting things off, and for how many chances he's already had. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: there is a limit. Marcus said it to himself first, and gently. Until tomorrow.
